name: Bamvələ
overview: The Bamvələ live on their ancestral land, forming the majority among the Gbaya, the Makaa and newcomers. An open society where the chief decides in assembly with his notables, they practise farming, fishing and a little trade, share dance and the mvet with the Beti, and make mbɔ̀l their emblematic dish.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, neighbouring the Gbaya and the Makaa; spouses learn each other's language.
Bamvələ is spoken in the Centre and South, and speakers live as far away as Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire.
People marry anyone, as long as the spouses love each other.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The group has always lived in the same place, on its ancestral land.
Large gatherings bring together all the Bamvələ at Nanga-Eboko or at Bertoua.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Decisions are taken in an assembly of the chief and notables; the chief decides after listening to everyone, and the assembly chooses what will be communicated to the population.
The chiefdom is passed from father to son or daughter, within the same family branch.
No avoidance rules: everyone is free, which keeps up good spirits.
Alliances and good relations with the Gbaya and the Makaa.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife settles with her husband after the celebration.
The boy becomes a man at around 18-21, when he is independent; the young woman, by marrying, or through responsibilities entrusted to her in the community.
No fixed age for marriage: the man must have a job.
Steps: meeting, presentation, marriage proposal, bride price, accompanying the wife.
The bride price includes ritual trials for the son-in-law: they want to see his commitment, without reproaching him for what he could not provide.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship; the dead may manifest themselves in dreams.
Birth is joy, happiness and proof of love.
Taboos: eating chimpanzee (said to cause herpes) or viper; incest within the Bassam family. Offences call for illness.
No divination practices.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men and women: farming, fishing, a little trade, with different tasks.
The chief distributes the land.
Few crafts (borrowed practice): rattan chairs, baskets, cups.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Oboom (bark garment, as among the Beti), kaba, wrapper and headscarf.
Traditional medicine is important and respected, notably for what the hospital does not cure (infertility, mystical ailments).
Beauty: the plump man, healthy-looking, with a natural complexion, who takes care of his wife; the natural woman who takes care of her husband.
Courtship: compliments, humour, ability to provide for needs; the woman respectful, presentable and dignified.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Songs in the language, mvet, tam-tam, balafon, horn.
Dances: bikutsi, ayanga, natchigal.
The harvest festival, discontinued, should be revived.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Bamvələ resemble the Beti of the Centre and South (clothing, marriage, absence of ancestor worship); an anecdote explains why mbɔ̀l is their traditional dish.

sections.title: The names
items: Men's names evoke ferocity, hardness, power; twins are called bon, and the child who follows them Beng.
The name is claimed by the family; it is not changed, as that would bring a curse.
Pseudonyms depend on each person's character and function.
Founding ancestor: Dang, “the one who surpassed everyone”, and Sazang, his strong-willed uncle.

lessons.title: Who are the Bamvələ? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bamvələ community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: Lower part of the meeting place/meetings

lessons.competence: Introduce the Bamvələ community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bamvələ community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bamvələ community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bamvələ community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bamvələ call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, neighbour of the Gbaya and the Makaa; spouses learn each other's language. • Bamvələ is spoken in the Centre and the South, and speakers live as far as Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire. • People marry with everyone, as long as the spouses love each other. • The group has always lived in the same place, on its ancestral land. • Large gatherings bring together all the Bamvələ at Nanga-Eboko or at Bertoua.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bamvələ live on their ancestral land, forming the majority among the Gbaya, the Makaa and newcomers. An open society where the chief decides in assembly with his notables, they practise farming, fishing and a little trade, share dance and the mvet with the Beti, and make mbɔ̀l their emblematic dish.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bamvələ community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bamvələ
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bamvələ, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bamvələ.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bamvələ, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bamvələ.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: mbɔ̀l, cucumber seed dish. • Drinks: matango (palm wine), raffia wine, kpata. • Men and women: farming, fishing, a little trade, with different tasks.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bamvələ mainly eat mbɔ̀l, cucumber-seed dishes. Traditional drinks: matango, raffia wine, kpata. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bamvələ: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Bamvələ
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Bamvələ welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Bamvələ family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Bamvələ welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Bamvələ family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Men's names evoke ferocity, hardness, power; twins are called bon, and the child who follows them Beng. • The name is claimed by the family; it is not changed, as that would be a source of curses. • Nicknames depend on each person's character and function. • Birth is joy, happiness and proof of love. • The boy becomes a man around 18-21, when he is independent; the young woman, on getting married, or through responsibilities entrusted to her in the community.

student.memo: Among the Bamvələ, traditional dances (bikutsi, ayanga, natchigal) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: mvet, tam-tam, balafon, horn. Festival(s): to be revived.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bamvələ
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bamvələ, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bamvələ. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bamvələ, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bamvələ. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men and women: farming, fishing, a little trade, with different tasks. • The chief allocates the land. • Few crafts (a borrowed practice): rattan chairs, baskets, cups.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men and women: farming, fishing, a little trade, with different tasks. The chief distributes the land.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bamvələ's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Bamvələ make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men and women: farming, fishing, a little trade, with different tasks. The chief distributes the land.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bamvələ
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bamvələ, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bamvələ. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bamvələ, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bamvələ. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship; the dead may appear in dreams. • Birth is joy, happiness and proof of love. • Taboos: eating chimpanzee (said to cause herpes) or viper; incest within the Bassam family. Offences bring illness. • No divination practices.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship; the dead may manifest themselves in dreams. Birth is joy, happiness and proof of love.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bamvələ (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Bamvələ believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: No ancestor worship; the dead may manifest themselves in dreams. Birth is joy, happiness and proof of love.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Bamvələ
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bamvələ and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bamvələ family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bamvələ greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bamvələ family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Bamvələ. • Greetings: Ó dámá = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); O dámá = morning greeting (one person); Balí dámá = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Dzial/pɔ́k, Ba, La, Nyi, Tán. • Founding ancestor: Dang, “the one who surpassed everyone”, and Sazang, his uncle with a strong character. • The Bamvələ resemble the Beti of the Centre and South (dress, marriage, absence of ancestor worship); an anecdote explains why mbɔ̀l is their traditional dish.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Bamvələ are the first steps towards communicating with the Bamvələ. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Bamvələ.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Bamvələ are the first steps towards communicating with the Bamvələ. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
